# GrabPoseAuthoring

**Class** · namespace `VRFramework.Core.Editors.Interaction` · assembly `VRFramework.Core.Editors` · [view source](https://git.cie-group.cz/vr-framework/vrf4/core/-/blob/main/Editor/Interaction/GrabPoseAuthoring.cs#L24)

The operations that shape a ghost hand where it stands, at the grip point it is going to hold.

A grip is two things: where the hand sits, and what its fingers do. The first is the grip
point, a transform an author drags in the scene. The second was fifteen bones to rotate one at
a time in the hierarchy, which is why nobody authored poses. Everything here exists to remove
that: close the hand onto the object and read the answer, curl a finger with one number, build
a fist, mirror the whole pose to the other hand.

"Close onto object" runs the same [`AutoPoseSolver`](/api/vrframework-interaction-runtime/AutoPoseSolver) the game runs, on the same
geometry, so what an author sees on the ghost is what the player's hand will do - and it is
seen at the object, without entering play mode. An authored grip usually starts as a solved
one that was then nudged.

### Begin(GripPoint, HandType) {#begin-grippoint-handtype}

Brings out a hand to author one pose on, at the root of the scene.

At the root, not under the object: a hand parented to the grabbable takes its scale, and
the same pose authored on a crate and on a crate half the size would be held by two
differently sized hands. It is temporary and never saved - what survives editing is the
[`GripPose`](/api/vrframework-interaction-runtime/GripPose) read off it.

### CloseOntoObject(GrabbableObject, CustomGrabPose, AutoPoseSettings, List\<FingerSolve>) {#closeontoobject-grabbableobject-customgrabpose-autoposesettings-fingersolve}

Closes the ghost's fingers onto the object, each stopping where it first meets a collider.

The far end of the travel is the fist the hand builds for itself, and the near end is
wherever the ghost is now - so solving a hand that has already been part-posed keeps that
work and only closes it the rest of the way.


### Mirror(CustomGrabPose, CustomGrabPose) {#mirror-customgrabpose-customgrabpose}

Poses one ghost as the mirror image of the other.

Each bone's rotation is taken relative to its own hand root, reflected across that root's
sagittal plane, and put back relative to the other root. Doing it through the roots rather
than by flipping the stored local rotations means it does not depend on the two rigs having
matching local bone axes, which mirrored skeletons routinely do not.

Reflecting a rotation across a plane reflects its axis and reverses its angle, which for a
quaternion about the x = 0 plane is (x, -y, -z, w).

Each bone then gets a fixed correction, so that mirroring a rig's own rest pose lands
exactly on the other hand's rest pose. Measured on the framework's own hands, the raw
reflection puts 23 of 24 bones within half a degree and the thumb metacarpal out by 10.8 -
the two hands were not modelled as exact mirrors of each other. That one bone carries the
whole thumb, so the error is worth removing rather than nudging back by hand every time.

Only the fingers are mirrored. Where the hand sits is the author's, and a hand reflected
through the object's own plane is only the right place to hold it when the object happens
to be symmetrical about that plane.

```csharp
public static int Mirror(CustomGrabPose from, CustomGrabPose to)
```

**Parameters**

| --- | --- | --- |
| `from` | [`CustomGrabPose`](/api/vrframework-interaction-runtime/CustomGrabPose) | The ghost already posed. |
| `to` | [`CustomGrabPose`](/api/vrframework-interaction-runtime/CustomGrabPose) | The ghost to write. |

**Returns** [`int`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.int32) - How many bones were mirrored.

### MirrorTo(GripPoint, CustomGrabPose) {#mirrorto-grippoint-customgrabpose}

Writes the mirror of a hand's grip into the object's grip for the other hand.

The fingers are mirrored properly, through each rig's own rest pose. Where the hand sits is
reflected across the grip point's own x = 0 plane, which is exactly right for a handle
symmetrical about that plane and a starting point for anything else - so it is offered as
a pose to look at and drag, not as one to trust.

```csharp
public static HandType? MirrorTo(GripPoint point, CustomGrabPose from)
```

### SetCurl(CustomGrabPose, FingerType, float) {#setcurl-customgrabpose-fingertype-single}

Curls one finger of the ghost, as a fraction of the way from open to closed.

The whole finger moves on one number, which is the point: a grip needs the index finger a
little more closed far more often than it needs one knuckle turned three degrees.

```csharp
public static int SetCurl(CustomGrabPose pose, FingerType finger, float amount)
```
